In 1981 a relative of mine was blindsided when her husband of many years announced that he was leaving her and their children for another woman. This successful New York accountant and business manager—his clients’ names now convey a faint period glamour, including the couturier Arnold Scaasi, who dressed several First Ladies, and Wilhelmina Cooper, whose Wilhemina Models agency allegedly supplied President Kennedy with women during his visits to Manhattan—had been plotting a divorce for some time. Methodically he’d asked his wife to sign documents that he assured her were routine paperwork she need not read, but which reassigned their joint assets to him alone. To make matters worse, he was being represented by another of his clients, the celebrity attorney Raoul Felder, whom Variety described as “America’s go-in-for-the-kill king of divorce” and the “shark of split.”

My relative was terrified of winding up penniless or even dead. Her husband, always prone to bullying, began to act ever more irrationally. He cut the brakes on her car at their suburban hilltop home, and after he moved out he tore off the oven door when she refused to bake cookies for him. He kept her on a bare minimum allowance, and all the divorce lawyers she approached required a substantial upfront retainer. As she detailed her desperate situation to me, my instinctive reaction was that one must fight fire with fire. And in those days there was nothing quite like the panic that ensued when an errant spouse received a lawyer’s letter from the firm of Saxe, Bacon & Bolan over the signature of Roy M. Cohn, Esq., widely known as New York’s most cutthroat power broker, a macher among machers, the fixer of all fixers.

During the heady 1980s I worked for Condé Nast and knew that Cohn remained the lifelong best friend of the magazine company’s chairman, S.I. Newhouse, Jr., whose split from his first wife, Jane Franke, Cohn had handled. My wife and I had been taken up socially by Si and his second wife, Victoria, and I learned that he went into his office at 4:00 AM to work uninterruptedly for several hours before his employees showed up. If you really needed to speak with Si—and the reason had better be good—you could call him then and he’d pick up the phone himself.

Thus I arrived at my Condé Nast office one day before dawn, got him on the line, explained my relative’s plight, and asked if he would intervene with Cohn to take her case. He said he’d do what he could, and within a day called back to say that Roy asked to meet with us at his office. “Take a teddy bear,” he added. “What?” I replied, thinking I’d misheard him. “Bring him a teddy bear,” he repeated, “He likes teddy bears.” OK, I thought to myself, do whatever the man says, and I duly headed to F.A.O. Schwarz to find a suitably impressive stuffed animal for our conference with Si’s boyhood pal.

When my relative and I arrived for our 11:00 AM appointment with Cohn at the Saxe, Bacon & Bolan offices on East 68th Street, Steiff plushie in hand, we were startled to find that behind the imposing limestone façade of this midblock Beaux-Arts mansion were interiors as shabby and barren as a Morningside Heights frat house. Cohn also lived there, above the store as it were, but the townhouse was owned by a shell company lest he lose some personal lawsuit. In 1964 Cohn and Thomas A. Bolan (a former federal prosecutor and a founder of New York State’s Conservative Party) bought out a respectable old Wall Street law firm, Saxe, Bacon & O’Shea. But Cohn was never a named partner. He much preferred to operate behind the scenes, as his heedless demeanor was about to reveal to us.

We were ushered upstairs to a large, sparsely furnished, wood-paneled salon on the piano nobile, and a few minutes later Cohn shambled into the room. Barefoot and dressed—or, more accurately, undressed—in a loosely tied, silk paisley dressing gown, he clearly was wearing nothing underneath. After he seated himself in a well-worn wing chair, his manspreading and leg-crossing stopped just short of full disclosure. He was deeply tanned, the color of a well-used baseball mitt, which made his penetrating aquamarine eyes stand out even more. They were so heavy-lidded that he appeared to be wide awake and half asleep at the same time, a disconcerting effect that this master manipulator habitually exploited to his advantage.

Advertisement

When my relative nervously presented him with the requisite stuffed animal he smiled wanly and said, “You know I collect teddy bears. Very nice.” He then set it aside, agreed to take her on as a client, and spoke with contempt of Raoul Felder. (I never learned how Felder or his client reacted to Cohn’s unanticipated involvement.) Aware that his supplicant had no cash because of her husband’s machinations, he said that payment could wait until the case was settled. Of course, Cohn added, he’d hand over day-to-day dealings to a younger member of the firm but would oversee everything himself. He then stood up, took the teddy, and left the room, robe flapping. Our audience was over in less than ten minutes. We were next introduced to a boyish-looking associate who was to be our primary contact, and we soon left the premises with a vague sense of having done something not quite kosher.

Thereupon followed days and weeks of silence from the law office, with countless unreturned phone messages that only increased our unease as nothing progressed. Although this entire saga transpired in less than a year, after six months’ inaction my relative had become so unnerved that she was ready to accept her husband’s draconian terms. To prevent that dire outcome, I offered to have the case assessed by an attorney recommended to me for her shrewd forensic analyses of other lawyers’ performance. After reviewing the paperwork, this expert concluded that Cohn’s firm was indeed slow-walking the matter, but she felt that my relative’s prospects were rather hopeless anyway. “Sometimes delaying is not such a bad thing,” she told me. “And as they say, you can always settle on the courthouse steps. But please get back to me when it’s over—I’m curious to know how this all plays out.”

Within a few weeks of that consultation, the plaintiff, who was not yet fifty, dropped dead of a heart attack. He had a history of cardiac disease and his wife had learned CPR to save him—but when he was stricken he was with his girlfriend. (To our family’s horror she crashed the funeral and threw herself on the coffin for good measure.) Because the divorce had not been finalized, the widow inherited everything, including his business, which she sold for its lucrative client list, an unexpected windfall. As one outspoken aunt commented a bit too loudly at the service, “This is the best thing that could have happened,” which others of us also thought but dared not say. My betrayed relative then wed a sweet-natured widower with whom she shared a happy second marriage that lasted nearly as long as her first.

Soon after fate rendered the divorce proceedings moot, she received an invoice from Saxe, Bacon & Bolan for $35,000 (more than $120,000 in current value). It contained no itemization, just the stunningly large sum. (According to American Scoundrel, “Unlike most lawyers, Roy did not keep track of billable hours.”) When she informed me that she had no intention of paying so much, I replied that this was one dispute I’d not get involved with, fearful that Cohn might complain to his friend Si about the deadbeat he’d sent him. With newfound assertiveness she told the firm’s junior associate that the fee was ridiculous, and the most she would offer was $7,500 (about $25,000 today), which she somehow calculated as a fair amount. Without skipping a beat he accepted, which made me wonder how Cohn’s office handled its finances. But as his friend Alan Dershowitz recalled in a PBS Frontline interview in 2018, “He would never set a fee in advance. After he did great favors for people, he would always say, ‘Pay me what you think it was worth.’”

Murray Kempton’s posthumous verdict on this dark prince of the city held that, “having been defeated in all his hopes for eminence, Cohn could only fall back on notoriety and return to being mercenary soldier for gangsters habitually disreputable or wives made transiently so by the ravenings of their thirst for revenge.” My relative, however, did not seek retribution but was fighting for survival, as distasteful as recourse to this guttersnipe of the law may have been. When the ashes to ashes and dust to dust finally settled, I contacted the consultant attorney as promised and reported the stunning denouement and providential resolution. “Well,” she replied, “I’ve always said that Roy Cohn runs a full-service operation.”

entries.title: Comics Relief
entries.summary: In late August, Coyote vs. Acme, a feature-length treatment of the eponymous coyote’s eternally thwarted efforts to eat the Road Runner, finally opened in theaters, years after the artless CEO of Warner Brothers Discovery determined never to release it. “Coyote vs. Acme takes a lesson from the darkness of Who Framed Roger Rabbit?,” Lucas Adams writes in […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In late August, Coyote vs. Acme, a feature-length treatment of the eponymous coyote’s eternally thwarted efforts to eat the Road Runner, finally opened in theaters, years after the artless CEO of Warner Brothers Discovery determined never to release it. “Coyote vs. Acme takes a lesson from the darkness of Who Framed Roger Rabbit?,” Lucas Adams writes in the NYR Online, “but asks: What if the bad guys had already won?” The result is “a barrage of clever, hilarious visuals”—“a courtroom stenographer dutifully transcribing the Tasmanian Devil’s incoherent ravings”—alongside a surprisingly wistful treatment of longing and desire deferred.

Adams is the editor of New York Review Comics, which publishes lost classics and new translations of comics, manga, and graphic novels—including work by Saul Steinberg, Joe Brainard, and Glen Baxter—for our sister book imprint. His writing, cartoons, and illustrations have appeared in The New Yorker and The Paris Review, and for The New York Review he has written about, among other subjects, speculative fiction, William Wegman, and Edward Gorey.

This week I wrote to Adams to ask him about the Looney Tunes, the comics industry, and growing up humorless.

Daniel Drake: What’s your history with the Looney Tunes? Did you grow up with them? Have you given them much critical thought in your adulthood? Most importantly, which ones do you plan to show to your young son first?

Lucas Adams: Unfortunately for everyone around me, I was humorless as a child. My parents bought me joke books and showed me movies like Monty Python and the Holy Grail (I cried at the end: they didn’t find the grail, and they were arrested for a crime they didn’t commit), but nothing seemed to amuse me much. So for a while I was pretty hostile to the unfairness of the world depicted in the Looney Tunes.

But I softened, eventually. My real entry points were Nineties iterations of the Tunes like Steven Spielberg Presents: Tiny Toon Adventures and Space Jam (my elementary school’s music teacher made us perform a coordinated dance to “I Believe I Can Fly” for our parents). Once I started actually watching the original Merrie Melodies shorts, around age twelve or so, I loved how each was its own world, especially the care that the animators put into the backgrounds, in particular the abstract southwestern setting for Coyote and Road Runner. I connected it with the landscapes Bill Watterson drew for his Spaceman Spiff Sunday strips in Calvin and Hobbes, which looked like the same dreamlike desert.

My son, Harold, is two and a half, and when he’s just a little bit older we’ll be on a strict regimen of the classics to get him started, like What’s Opera Doc?

Your review makes a point of putting this latest Looney Tunes live action movie into a lineage running from Roger Rabbit through Space Jam. As a comics editor, how do you find the art style has changed or been adapted over time? They are still drawing the same characters in a rather circumscribed, branded fashion, but do you see any kind of evolution or variation over time?

It’s hard not to feel the intrusion of digital slickness in the look of the characters in Coyote vs. Acme compared to the original animations.

That said, one of my favorite details about Coyote vs. Acme was something Will Forte mentioned at the screening I attended at the Museum of the Moving Image. The filmmakers had brought in the legendary puppeteer Dave Barclay to work on the film. Barclay has worked on Jim Henson projects like Labyrinth and Fraggle Rock, and he was one of the puppeteers who operated Jabba the Hutt in Return of the Jedi. For Coyote vs. Acme, Barclay built a coyote puppet for the actors to perform with, so even when that digital sheen on some of the cartoons had me missing the texture of the original animation, it was exciting to know that the hands that helped moved Jabba contributed to the bodily humor and tragedy of the digital Coyote.

How did you get started as a comics editor? What were you doing before that?

My first real comics editing gig was at the online magazine The Rumpus, where I was an assistant comics editor under Paul Madonna. At first I mostly posted strips, but then I had the opportunity to conduct interviews and recruit cartoonists for the site. Paul was a good mentor, and I got a taste for curation from him and a model for thinking about how different comics best fit together.

When I moved to New York in 2010, I was drawing my own comics and working at a lot of food trucks (at various times: dumplings, lobster rolls, ice cream sandwiches). In 2013 I landed an internship at New York Review Books (if memory serves, it was only supposed to last six weeks). I became friends with two of my colleagues, Gabriel Winslow-Yost and Evan Johnston. We’d get drinks after work and talk comics. In the fall of 2013 I pitched them on an idea I’d had since I first read McSweeney’s Quarterly issue 13 (the all-comics issue) in high school: What if NYRB published comics? I’d always been shocked that McSweeney’s or another small literary publisher hadn’t really pursued the market. In the 2000s comics publishers, much like NYRB Classics, had started putting out more exciting reprints and translations: rediscoveries like Fantagraphics’ Fletcher Hanks reissues in 2008 and Drawn and Quarterly’s English translations of Yoshihiro Tatsumi’s excellent midcentury manga in 2006. My sense was that there was more out there. Gabe and Evan liked the idea too, and we took it to the NYRB Classics series founder Edwin Frank. He was intrigued, and after we put together a catalog of possible titles, we got started for real in September 2014.

Advertisement

Eighteen months later NYRC published our first title—Mark Beyer’s Agony, an acrid, funny bit of despair from the Eighties—which makes this year our tenth anniversary. I’m very grateful that we’ve gotten to keep on keeping on publishing comics since then. Our forty-eighth title, Dash Shaw’s Like Swimmers, just came out at the end of August, the day before Coyote vs. Acme premiered. 

The NYRC catalog is multifarious—running from single-panel gag comics to book-length epics, from pen or pencil line drawings to rich oils or watercolors, and every conceivable trim size. Before you started editing the imprint, where did your taste in comics tend? What first drew you in?

I was a newspaper comics kid (Peanuts, The Far Side, Calvin and Hobbes, even Doonesbury, eventually), but when I hit high school my reading picked up with David Boring by Daniel Clowes, Persepolis by Marjane Satrapi, a very weird Nightmare Alley adaptation by Spain Rodriguez, and anything that Cody’s Books in Berkeley had on display, including, crucially, the McSweeney’s Quarterly Number 13, which was the portal to everything I’ve done since.

Later, I went to Reed College, which has a student-run comics library. The stuff there filled in a lot of gaps in my reading, especially for collections that would have been out of my price range as a student. I can admit this now: I skipped a final presentation given by some classmates in fall 2007 so I could go finish reading the full-color Epic Comics edition of the Akira manga. One of the great reading experiences of my life.

When we finally started NYRC, I was very conscious that my tastes and range were still limited. So I had to go ask for advice and get suggestions, which turned into one of the best parts of the job. I have found that there is real power in asking and finding out more. So much of what I know now came from people like Dan Nadel, Nicole Rudick, Sammy Harkham, and Ed Park taking the time to talk to me about comics and what they liked. A true gift.

Are there any comics that NYRC has, for whatever reason, been unable to publish that you’d like to see brought back to the public anyway? What are some great lost classics?

I really hope someone is able to print a new edition of Captain Goodvibes by Tony Edwards. It’s a comic about an irradiated pork chop that becomes a surfing pig. The strip was published in the Australian surf magazine Tracks, mostly in the 1970s. It’s just some of the most beautiful, intricate draftsmanship in comics paired with the most outrageous humor of the Seventies. There was an Australian edition that collected a selection of the strips more than ten years ago, and I was in touch with Edwards a couple times over the last decade, but nothing has ever come to pass. I might try again soon.

What’s your all-time favorite Coyote and Road Runner gag?

Road Runner running into a painting of a tunnel that he shouldn’t be able to, and Coyote attempting the same thing and crashing into the rock face. There was nothing more mind-boggling for overly serious young Lucas than seeing this play out. It suggested there were worlds beyond the ones I understood. Plus, it’s very funny.

entries.title: In Billy’s Band
entries.summary: Among the many astonishing moments in Get Back—the 2021 documentary that Peter Jackson made from rehearsal footage of the Beatles in January 1969, bickering like siblings as they created some of the songs that would find immortality on the albums Let It Be and Abbey Road—one of the most magical involves the underappreciated musician Billy […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Among the many astonishing moments in Get Back—the 2021 documentary that Peter Jackson made from rehearsal footage of the Beatles in January 1969, bickering like siblings as they created some of the songs that would find immortality on the albums Let It Be and Abbey Road—one of the most magical involves the underappreciated musician Billy Preston. After a few years of studio wizardry, during which the increasingly estranged band members sometimes laid down separate tracks at separate times, the Beatles had decided to try to recapture some of the fun of their early days by recording together in person. That meant, however, that there was no one left to play the Fender Rhodes, an electric piano that came on the market in 1965 and was a new toy in their studio—and they wanted its sound on the recordings. “We need somebody else,” John Lennon says in the film, “a guy who plays piano all the time.”

The next day Preston—in London while touring with Ray Charles—drops by the studio, invited by George Harrison to say hello. When Lennon asks Preston to sit in on the Rhodes, he coolly agrees. Then his delight and disbelief escape in a giggle. The Beatles are working on the gospel-rock song “I’ve Got a Feeling,” and after Paul McCartney sings the title phrase, Preston answers on the Rhodes like a church organist affirming a preacher. Sliding up to a chord the way a guitarist bends a note, he blurs major and minor, entering the emotional in-between zone of the blues. The Rhodes’s pinched electric cry brings out the ache within the song’s rapture, and the light-fingered riff that Preston plays next ties the chord into the song’s marching momentum. McCartney’s eyes go wide.

“You’re in the group,” Lennon says, and over the coming days Preston records several songs with them. Similar small but perfect adjustments spill from his fingers with native fluency: a blues walkdown in “Get Back,” a concluding solo on “Don’t Let Me Down” that responds to the song’s desperate pleas with waltz-like reassurance. Even more remarkable than the music is Preston’s effect on the Beatles. Instead of squabbling, they’re laughing, quoting their old songs, telling stories from the early days in Hamburg in 1962, when they were the scruffy opening act for one of their heroes, Little Richard, and Preston, then sixteen, was playing organ in Little Richard’s band. Lennon now suggests bringing him on as “a fifth Beatle.”

In Get Back you can see how easily Preston finds a place for himself in the music. But you can also see that he isn’t a part of the band’s banter, the funny voices, the inside jokes and coded references, much less the fraught love language between Lennon and McCartney (a bond illuminated as never before in Ian Leslie’s recent book John & Paul: A Love Story in Songs). Still, as Lennon remarks, Preston has given them “a lift”—all the way to the top of the building, where he joins the band for the rooftop concert that will turn out to be their last live performance together. Later, when the Beatles released the single “Get Back,” they credited “The Beatles with Billy Preston,” a co-billing they gave to no other musician. Get Back’s nearly eight hours of evidence leave the impression that the credit honors a larger contribution—that if Preston had not shown up at the studio that day, we might not have Let It Be or Abbey Road at all.

When footage of Preston recording with the Beatles appears in Paris Barclay’s new documentary, Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It, it demonstrates something different, and larger, than Preston’s connection to the world’s most famous band. As the drummer Bill Maxwell explains in the film, “Billy didn’t just have perfect pitch, he had perfect anticipation.” It didn’t matter if Preston had never heard a song before; he could immediately play along. This skill helped turn him into what Barclay has described as a Zelig figure in pop music history. He played with Mahalia Jackson and Sly Stone, Aretha Franklin and The Band. After recording with the Beatles he recorded with the Rolling Stones, a double coup that made him a sideman at the center of the cross-Atlantic, cross-racial exchange of rock and roll.

But Preston, who died in 2006, was also a child prodigy and a solo artist with his own hits, including “That’s the Way God Planned It,” the 1969 song that gives the documentary its title. Ray Charles once introduced him as the young man he wanted to carry on the work he started, and that’s what Preston did. Along with Stone, he pushed Charles’s gospel-derived rhythm and blues into a kind of funk that could cohabitate with flower-power pop-rock. By the 1980s and 1990s, however, he had flamed out in addiction and jail time. That’s the Way God Planned It tries to explain why. Its answers have to do less with the familiar story of racism in rock than with the Black church and the closet—what one old friend of Preston’s calls the “things that he held in.”

Advertisement

Born in 1946, Preston was raised in the church. His mother played piano for a Los Angeles congregation, and he was accompanying choirs and preachers on piano and organ by the time he was six. An early mentor was James Cleveland, the so-called King of Gospel who invented its modern big-choir sound. (You can see Cleveland at full force with another of his protégées, Aretha Franklin, in the miraculous film of her 1972 return to gospel, Amazing Grace.) Preston entered show business early, too. At eleven, he portrayed the young W.C. Handy in the 1958 biopic St. Louis Blues. Nat King Cole, who played the adult Handy, invited Preston onto his TV show—the first national program to have a Black host. After Preston played his own composition, “Billie’s Boogie,” grinning proudly at the camera, the two performed “Blueberry Hill” together, trading off on organ and vocals like peers or maybe father and son. “I know that you have a very excellent career ahead of you,” Cole told the boy, publicly anointing him.

By the time Preston met Little Richard, the holy roller who had helped establish the rapturous sound of rock and roll with songs like “Long Tall Sally” had renounced secular music. He hired the teenaged Preston as the organist for a gospel tour in Europe in 1962. But when Richard heard the contrast between the silence his gospel songs received and the ecstatic screams induced by the opening act his promoters had hired for him in Britain—the gospel-turned-soul star Sam Cooke—Richard brought back his old songs, and Preston played along, rocking on the organ for what he recalled as the first time.

After the Hamburg leg of the Little Richard tour, Cooke hired Preston to bring some juke-joint organ grease to his after-hours masterpiece Night Beat (1963), and Cooke’s SAR label released Preston’s debut album, 16 Yr. Old Soul (1963). That album and his next three, including the only slightly hyperbolic The Most Exciting Organ Ever (1965), were almost entirely instrumental, but as a member of the house band for the TV variety show Shindig, Preston also sang and danced—not smoothly like Jackie Wilson, the “Lonely Teardrops” singer who could fall to his knees with feather softness, but less controlled, like James Brown getting the spirit. It was Preston’s impersonation of Ray Charles that prompted Charles to hire him.

After Preston helped the Beatles in the Get Back sessions, they returned the favor by signing him to their Apple label. Harrison produced solo albums that presented Preston as a pop star, starting with That’s the Way God Planned It (1969). Over the next years Preston released a few chart-topping singles—such as “Nothing from Nothing,” a bouncy song with honky tonk piano that he performed on the first episode of Saturday Night Live in 1975—and wrote “You Are So Beautiful,” the 1974 song that gave Joe Cocker one of his most enduring hits. In Preston’s original version, on his album The Kids & Me, the backing of gospel piano, voices, and strings is combined with a synthesizer like those heard on Stevie Wonder tracks from the same era. Developing that forward-searching sound while alluding to God and Black Pride, Preston’s Seventies albums fit alongside what artists like Wonder, Stone, and Marvin Gaye were doing then. Preston even contributed the title song to a Blaxploitation film, Slaughter (1972).

At the same time, he was contributing to solo projects by Harrison, Lennon, and Ringo Starr, and joining the Rolling Stones on a run of albums including Sticky Fingers (1971) and Exile on Main Street (1972). The bass line on the Stones’ 1978 disco riff “Miss You” was Preston’s idea. Unlike B.B. King, Chuck Berry, or Ike and Tina Turner—Black heroes who were segregated into the supporting-act slot when they appeared with the Stones—Preston performed as a member of the band who was occasionally allowed to play his own songs, among them the futuristically funky “Outa-Space,” with the Stones backing him. He wore a gigantic Afro wig that he liked, he said, because when he took it off, he “could just be a regular guy.”

Advertisement

Fitting in offstage was perilous. Preston developed addictions to Courvoisier, cocaine, and, eventually, crack, and it couldn’t have helped his mental stability when he discovered his girlfriend, the model Kathy Silva, in bed with his friend and collaborator Sly Stone, who married Silva at Madison Square Garden not long after. Over the next few decades, Preston slipped down a slide of self-destruction. In 1991, while on probation for a drunk-driving conviction, he was arrested for sexually assaulting a sixteen-year-old boy. That charge was dropped in a plea deal and his sentence was reduced to a term at a rehab facility, but he was later sent to jail for violating his parole and for insurance fraud after he set fire to his home.

After years in and out of rehab, he finally succumbed to kidney disease and pericarditis. But before that, friends tried to save him. In the early 2000s Eric Clapton vouched for him in a sobriety program so that he could join Clapton’s band on tour. Decades earlier the guitar god had played on Preston’s albums and Preston had played on his. In the documentary, Clapton says that Preston was “the most important person on just about every track,” able to make a great band sound even greater, to guide without stealing the spotlight. “I was in Billy’s band,” he says.

What did Preston hold in? David Ritz, the coauthor of autobiographies of Ray Charles, Marvin Gaye, Aretha Franklin, and many others, says in Barclay’s documentary that he couldn’t get far with Preston—even after years of friendship, it was difficult to draw him out. But Barclay coaxed some interview subjects into discussing, uncomfortably, awkwardly, what Keith Richards had revealed in his 2010 memoir: Preston was queer. They mention the “nephews” and “cousins” he would bring on tour, but also that “you wouldn’t know he was gay.”

“Nephews” and “cousins” were standard euphemisms in the closeted world of the Black church. Another was “the children,” a term of somewhat condescending affection for the many queer people—stereotypically the boy playing organ or the choir director—who found a confusing mix of solace, strength, and self-hatred in a church that condemned their sexuality. In the words of the gospel historian Anthony Heilbut (who doesn’t appear in Barclay’s film): “Without lesbians and gay men there could be no gospel music.”

In Ritz’s biography of Franklin, published eight years after Preston’s death, he quotes Preston addressing the topic with rare frankness. “Everyone knew that my mentor, James Cleveland, was gay,” Preston said. “In the neighborhood, they made you ashamed of being gay, but in the church you were almost proud to be part of the gay elite of musicians. Along with the preachers, we were the people who kept the church going…. God is in the grooves.” It’s now commonly recognized that much of Little Richard’s sound and showmanship derived from the gender-fluid aesthetic of gospel, like the high-pitched “whoo!” he cribbed from the gospel queen Marion Williams and claimed to have taught to McCartney in Hamburg.

Barclay’s film doesn’t delve much into that history, but it does dwell on a secret beneath the secret, first revealed in a 2010 BBC Radio 4 documentary: that Preston was “taken advantage of” or “touched,” more than once, as a child touring with his mother. “No one knew what had transpired except us inner circle family people,” the singer Merry Clayton says in the film over photos of Preston in the innocence of youth. “He’d have that smile, but his heart would be broken.”

His last manager, Joyce Moore, tells of how he finally admitted he was gay during a rehab group therapy session in late 2005. It was the first time, she says, that he had spoken those words to strangers. “I knew then that he was never going to have to look over his shoulder again,” she recalls. Four days later he fell into a coma from which he never awoke.

The appearance in the film of Clayton—best known for wailing “Rape! Murder!” on the Stones’ “Gimme Shelter”—might suggest a point of view like that of 20 Feet from Stardom (2013), the documentary about her and other stellar backup singers, or Standing in the Shadows of Motown (2002), which gave faces and names to the musicians in the record label’s invaluable house band: a widening of the lens to include more than just the stars. And Preston’s connection to Little Richard might have helped the film bring up the issue of misplaced credit, much as Richard sometimes did when he justifiably reclaimed recognition as one of the true architects and originators of rock and roll.

But while That’s the Way God Planned It makes a few feints in those directions, the questions about credit are aimed less at the Beatles and the Stones than at Sly Stone. Sly stole Billy’s funk, Ritz says. Well, maybe, in a limited way. The two musicians were collaborating as early as the mid-Sixties, and Preston played on Stone’s “There’s a Riot Goin’ On.” Despite Preston’s sunny spirit, he wasn’t really a natural front man. He was more at home behind the keyboard, and his showmanship was musical: on YouTube, you can find videos of him on a Hammond B-3, expressing a fiery sermon or a two-part Bach invention, dancing all over the keys and the foot pedals at once. None of his immensely enjoyable albums have the paradigm-shifting creativity of those by Stone or the Beatles—or even other top session musicians, like Isaac Hayes, who were beginning to put out their own music at the same time.

The chameleon who could play along with everyone was also a cypher. He often wrote lyrics about an absence: a song that “ain’t got no melody,” a dance that “ain’t got no steps,” the Lear-like phrase “nothin’ from nothin’ leaves nothin’.” Something is always shrouded. Where Ray Charles famously took the sex in the blues strand of gospel’s DNA and made it explicit—refitting “It Must Be Jesus” as “I Got a Woman”—Preston made the sexual charge tacit again.

The most persuasive argument of Barclay’s film is that most of the songs Preston wrote were praise songs—not just the obvious ones, like that title number or “With You I’m Born Again,” his hit duet with Syreeta Wright. For Preston, music and the search for love were inextricably wound up with faith. To the end he called himself a servant of God, an instrument for the Lord.

“The black church is about truth-telling,” he told Ritz. “Ain’t no shame in crying in church. Ain’t no shame in moaning low and shouting high.” That truth-telling had clear limits but also clear avenues of expression. Heilbut once explained why closeted queer people might be attracted to gospel over secular songs: “Why sing disingenuously about one kind of emotion—sexual love—when all the others were yours to intimate, convey, and command?”

Who is the “you” in “You Are So Beautiful”? Sam Moore of Sam and Dave recalled telling Preston how useful the song was for picking up women, only to have Preston inform him that he had composed it in honor of his mother. The version most people know is Cocker’s. Barclay shows footage from the 1985 TV special “Motown Returns to the Apollo,” in which Cocker, accompanied by Preston at the piano, begins the song in his characteristic vulnerable growl, his version of blue-eyed soul. But Cocker is soon joined by Patti LaBelle in a plume helmet hairdo. Her voice leaps into the “whoo”s that Little Richard took from Marion Williams. She dances and shakes and brings the song back to church. When she kisses Preston on the cheek, he smiles. God is in the grooves, and however much LaBelle gestures at Cocker, her “you” is the Lord. It could also be Preston.

entries.title: ‘I Wish You Love’
entries.summary: On the day after she graduated high school, in 1964, Dolly Parton left her hometown of Locust Ridge, Tennessee, to head for Nashville, just over two hundred miles west and a world apart. Six years later she returned to her alma mater, Sevier County High School, to give a concert, which was recorded as her […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On the day after she graduated high school, in 1964, Dolly Parton left her hometown of Locust Ridge, Tennessee, to head for Nashville, just over two hundred miles west and a world apart. Six years later she returned to her alma mater, Sevier County High School, to give a concert, which was recorded as her first live album, A Real Live Dolly. The event was also a fundraiser, inaugurating the Dolly Parton Scholarship Foundation, which was to fund local students’ college tuition and purchase musical equipment for the school’s band.

By then, at twenty-four, Parton had released five solo albums and four albums recorded with the country music impresario Porter Wagoner. She’d joined his nationally televised variety show in 1967, and they’d become one of the most popular country-singing duos in the US. By the standards of the music and television business, she wasn’t exactly rich (for the seven years she worked on Wagoner’s weekly television show, her salary was around $60,000 a year), but compared to the extreme poverty of her childhood, she was a huge success. She’d come home to spread the wealth. “The foundation is a project for which she has great plans,” the album’s liner notes promised. Like many people Parton knew growing up, her father could neither read nor write, so encouraging literacy and education as a path to economic stability was a cause close to her heart, the impetus for a lifetime of philanthropy that would economically transform the region. (Her theme park, Dollywood, opened in 1986, making Pigeon Forge a major tourist hub; her Imagination Library, started in 1996, has to date sent more than three million free books to children around the world, once a month from birth until they’re five years old.)

At the concert Dolly was introduced by a local radio host, Cas Walker, who’d been having her as a guest on his show since she was ten years old. She opened with the silly-sweet songs her audience might have remembered hearing when she was a kid, as well as her first hit in Nashville, “Dumb Blonde”—“Just because I’m blonde, don’t think I’m dumb/Cause this dumb blonde ain’t no-oo-body’s fool”—followed by a suite of duets with Wagoner and a gospel song dedicated to her parents. She also sang a couple of her solo songs, already marked by the clever pathos of her distinctive songwriting voice, including the understated feminist anthem “Just Because I’m a Woman” and the premiere of a song that she identified with for the rest of her life, “Coat of Many Colors.”

The song’s premise is simple: it’s getting cold and the narrator needs winter clothes. The family is poor, so her mother stitches together a coat from rags, relating the story of Joseph in the book of Genesis while she sews. But being singled out as special has its risks, because of course she’s teased at school—the other children know the true reason her coat is patchwork:

They didn’t understand it, and I tried to make them see

That one is only poor only if they choose to be.

Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be

In my coat of many colors, my mama made for me.

The song captures much that defines Parton’s music: a preternatural dexterity with words as they are spoken; effortless rhymes and melodies that develop into complex narratives; a profound sense of identification with being different or looked down upon (whether as a woman or a poor person or a child or uneducated or a southerner); a commitment to a moral universe beyond materialism and money; and the belief that we make the world, other people, and ourselves beautiful and precious through love.

The vast outpouring of grief and tribute after Parton’s death at eighty late last month owes much to the fact that she was probably the kindest genius America ever had—all the more astonishing because her genius and her kindness were inextricable from each other. She was loved as deeply, and seemingly for the same reasons, on rodeo grounds and in gay bars, in rural towns and major cities, and across the extremes of the political spectrum. Her advocacy for loving the poor, welcoming the stranger, and bestowing generosity had its roots in her authentic, nondogmatic Christian faith, which over the decades put her at increasing odds with her country’s politicized Christianity and partisan polarization.

One has to imagine that whoever had laughed at Parton in elementary school was there in the packed auditorium that evening in Sevier County. The whole concert is a summary of her life’s story up to that moment, performed for those who knew her when. But it wasn’t like she was particularly comfortable there either, as she told an interviewer a few years later: “I never felt I belonged. Never belonged in my whole life, even as a little kid. I was just different and so I never really found my place till I moved to Nashville and got in the music business. That was my real place, so I fit in.” And like Joseph the Redeemer she returns; the coat of many colors, once an occasion for mockery, was in fact a blessing twice over, first as proof of her mother’s love and then as her art.

Advertisement

Growing up in rural east Tennessee provided a deep well of experience that Parton drew upon for thousands of songs. Small-town people know a lot about one another’s business, the best and the worst, and her songwriting reveals her to be a particularly sensitive observer. Throughout the Sixties she wrote a number of spooky ballads about young women who’d been loved and abandoned. “The Bridge” (1968) is told by a bereft woman recalling a failed romance, standing on the edge and overlooking a river: “From the bridge, I see reflections/in the waters far below.” “Here is where it started,” she sings, “and here is where I’ll end it,” at which point the song abruptly stops. In the aching “Down From Dover” (1970), another betrayed girl waiting for her faithless lover to return describes the seasons changing as her pregnancy comes to term: “The sun behind a cloud just casts a crawling shadow o’er the fields of clover/And time is running out for me, I wish that he would hurry down from Dover.” (He doesn’t—the baby is stillborn.)

Even when her tales are fully gothic—a malignant orphanage burned down by its charges in “Evening Shade” (1969) or a woman involuntarily admitted to a mental hospital by a sinister man in “Daddy Come and Get Me” (1970)—the predicaments and sorrows she describes are just a few degrees of intensity away from real life as it is lived all around her. When Parton writes about more quotidian scenes—a love triangle, a late romance, a middle-aged divorce—they’re emotionally subtle and resolutely adult, in a way that seems largely absent from contemporary music, pop, country, or otherwise.

Take what might seem to be the hyperbolic promise of the mega-hit “I Will Always Love You.” Both a “thank you” and a “goodbye” to Wagoner as Parton left his TV show and their collaboration in 1974, it is a break-up song disguised as a love song, and vice versa: “If I should stay/I would only be in your way/So I’ll go, but I know,/I’ll think of you each step of the way.” In the singing she attenuates the vowels—stay/way, know/go—which anticipates the melodic expansion between the “I” and “you” in the chorus, each word rhyming only with itself through repetition, as though the voice and feeling are enlarging to meet the growing space between the singer and her subject. Moreover, that ever-expanding “I” and “you” are the same note, the melody created by the four chords cycling beneath them—loves goes on forever, as the lovers go their separate ways. Formally, the song is so clean as to be transparent. Emotionally, it’s about neither severance nor celebration but the recognition that sometimes things just don’t work out. The song ends with a semi-spoken prayer: “I hope life/treats you kind,/and I hope that you have all you ever dreamed of/and I wish you joy and happiness/but above all of this I wish you love”—a sentiment bordering on cosmic empathy.

When Parton left Wagoner it was to pursue her solo career, which she thought could be much bigger than country music. It was a potentially treacherous transition, and she made it with aplomb. In 1977 she released her nineteenth solo album, Here You Come Again, explicitly aimed at the pop audience and propelled by the good-hearted intoxication of Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil’s title track—pure Brill Building bubblegum—which reached number 3 on the pop music charts. The second single, which also made the pop top 20, was Parton’s original, twangy, disco-inflected “Two Doors Down,” about getting over being sad and shy to find the fun that’s waiting for you (“because two doors down they’re laughing and drinking and having a party”). On the B-side, “It’s All Wrong, but It’s All Right,” about the pleasures of casual sex, she retains the emotional complexity and authenticity found in her country music:

Hello, are you free tonight?

I like your looks, I love your smile

Could I use you for a while?

It’s all wrong, but it’s all right.

She even keeps the high weirdness of her ghost ballads on “Me and Little Andy,” about a little girl and her puppy, abandoned by a mother and fleeing a drunk father, who take shelter from a storm with a good-natured stranger before the two die in their sleep; Parton sings parts of the dialogue in the child’s high voice. Perhaps most surprising, given the rest of the album, is “God’s Coloring Book,” a tender paean to a solitary communion with the divinity through nature—“Then I turn my face toward the sky/and say a silent prayer/Though God doesn’t speak to me/I see him everywhere.” In an album self-consciously engineered to introduce her to the mainstream, Parton demonstrated that she wasn’t leaving anything behind. The Appalachian Mountains, gospel, folk, disco, sex, God: in her music, it all exists in harmony.

Advertisement

Parton’s earliest appearances on the Porter Wagoner show capture her in Sixties country-girl drag with a blonde beehive and form-fitting shift dresses. Wagoner himself was known for a towering pompadour and outlandishly colored suits with sequins and rhinestones, a kind of country-western surrealism. Matching then outpacing him, Parton’s voluminous hair grew more sculptural, her outsized physical proportions accentuated with glittering costumes, her makeup heavier and brighter, until she arrived at an almost cartoon image of more-is-more femininity. The disparity between the high artifice of her appearance and the authenticity of her personality—not to mention the reality of her artistry—became a dialectic that drove the public’s fascination.

Look at Parton’s performance at the Grand Old Opry in 1969, featured in the documentary The Nashville Sound, stacked, spangled, playing her guitar, and singing a sad song about the boy she left back home: the faces in the audience are in utter disbelief, men’s mouths agog. All her career she used her appearance as a disarming joke, in control of the dazzle camouflage of gender, race, and class, often repeating her signature one-liner “it costs a lot of money to look this cheap.” As late as her 2008 country-pop album Backwoods Barbie, Parton was teasing out this dichotomy, playing, on the title song, the image of the infamous inanimate doll against the inner life of the real living person: “I’ve always been misunderstood because of how I look/Don’t judge me by the cover cause I’m a real good book/So read into it what you will, but see me as I am/The way I look is just a country girl’s idea of glam.” It’s a conceptual somersault: as astonishing as Parton’s appearance is, in fact because of its supreme construction, she is forever reminding us that when it comes to things that really matter, appearances have everything and almost nothing to do with it.

Riding this paradox of self and image, Parton catapulted to superstardom with her acting debut in the feminist blockbuster (another seeming oxymoron) 9 to 5 (1980), where she shares an intoxicating chemistry with her costars Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda. Parton is sweet and strong and funny and gorgeous as Doralee, a secretary dodging her boss’s advances with jokes until she can’t anymore—a character, like all her acting roles, that seemed to be an extension of “Dolly” the offscreen persona. She wrote the theme song, the famous typewriting-clacking opening conceived by rhythmically strumming her acrylic nails. The tune is so catchy, and by now so well known, it’s easy to forget how many words there are and how quickly they flow in the rush of getting to work:

Tumble out of bed and I stumble to the kitchen

Pour myself a cup of ambition

And yawn and stretch and try to come to life

Jump in the shower and the blood starts pumpin’

Out on the street, the traffic starts jumpin’

With folks like me on the job from nine to five.

The song served as the title track for a concept album released with the movie, 9 to 5 and Odd Jobs, that mixed original songs with a number of covers about labor, balancing the indignities of work against the pride of making a living, placing coal mining (“Dark as a Dungeon”) in the same category as sex work (“House of the Rising Sun”). A touching rendition of Woody Guthrie’s “Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos),” about a plane crash that killed some thirty Mexican laborers as they were being deported (“Who are these dear friends all scattered like dry leaves?/The radio said, ‘they were just deportees’”), portrays a simple humanity that qualifies as “woke” by today’s standards. Her own synth-hymn “Working Girl” blends vignettes about everywomen, dressed in guises from a pushup bra to a power suit to a uniform: “She’s a working girl, she is single and free/She’s a mother and wife and she’s proud to be/A working girl.” Much like her crossover album, where the provocation of a young woman singing about her own sexual desire can rest alongside her reverence for God, a collection of songs that places the explicitly gendered labor of women on an equal footing with more familiar sites of class struggle, performed as the most lovable mainstream pop, would be recognized as radical if Parton didn’t make it seem like a simple, uncontroversial description of reality.

Through movies and songs like these and an ever-growing presence on talk shows and in other public appearances, she developed a diverse and die-hard audience, especially among women and queer people. Her public statements on rights for LBGTQ+ communities were clear and consistent, explicitly citing the Christian value of accepting everyone as they are. “Travelin’ Thru,” the theme song she wrote and performed for the film Transamerica (2005), situates the experience of being trans within the loving embrace of Christ: “God made me for a reason and nothin’ is in vain/Redemption comes in many shapes with many kinds of pain/Oh, sweet Jesus, if you’re listenin’, keep me ever close to you/As I’m stumblin’, tumblin’, wanderin’, as I’m travelin’ through.” When she sings in the chorus that the protagonist is “like a poor wayfarin’ stranger that they speak about in song,” she’s riffing on one of the most powerful entries in the American songbook, “Wayfaring Stranger,” a folk and gospel standard with origins in African American spirituals. Parton summons the musical and spiritual foundations of the country in support of a ballad about queer people living their lives as best as they can, like everyone else. (You can hear the almost chilling intensity of her feeling for “Wayfaring Stranger” when she sings it on her 1994 live concert album Heartsongs.)

As she aged her high bell-like soprano acquired a razor’s edge, while her technical skills as a writer and musician reached new levels of virtuosity, culminating in a trilogy of bluegrass albums: The Grass Is Blue (1999), Little Sparrow (2001), and Halos and Horns (2002). These efforts were a stripped-down, amped-up musical return to the sounds of her childhood, blending Appalachian folk music with bluegrass and gospel. Widely acclaimed, the first won her a Grammy for best bluegrass album. It further endeared her to exacting Americana audiences, with the reviewer in Country Music proclaiming, “Her rigorous attention to craft and articulation, deep blues sensibility and emotional range have few matches anywhere.” With this added richness to her voice she revisits ballads of her youth like “Down from Dover,” this time with the wisdom of an older woman, and writes new ones like “Little Sparrow,” about a woman who, crushed like a little bird by a false lover, turns the same bird into an image of vengeance and transcendence. Covers of popular songs are transformed into devotional music, from the alt-rock group Collective Soul’s “Shine” to a rendition of Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven” where her voice crescendos into a psychedelic swirl of plucking banjos and gospel choir, adding her own lyrical riffs to the end: “Oh the great almighty dollar, leaves you lonely, lost, and hollow/You can’t fool yourself forever, you’ve got to work to get to heaven.”

Her sparkling rainbow-colored exterior was always an ingenious means of protection for a deep interiority. Despite the half-century of her fame, almost nothing is known about the nature of her long marriage or her closest friendships. She was acutely aware that she could take credit for her seemingly tireless work ethic but not for her extraordinary gifts, for which she was continuously grateful. This is the source of her deep goodness and flowing generosity. For her the space of creativity was itself the sacred, which is why she referred to the work of songwriting as entering the “god zone” or “spirit zone.” That place of communion required solitude yet was beyond the single self, a place to observe life in a kind of prayer. The purest portrait of who Dolly Parton was and what she valued as an artist and human being, from beginning to end, was already contained in a lyric she wrote in the early Sixties, before she even left home:

Words can’t describe what I feel inside

When I see the beauty in each coming day

What my eyes behold can’t be bought or sold

And everything’s beautiful in its own way.

entries.content:
In “The Art of the Interview,” season four of the podcast The Critic and Her Publics, Merve Emre speaks with top writers and journalists to discuss the subtle skill of conducting an interview. The Review is collaborating with Lit Hub to publish transcripts and recordings of each episode.



We try to end each season of The Critic and Her Publics with a little twist on our theme—something different and, often, a little risky or uncomfortable. Our final guest, Anna Silman, interviewed and profiled me for Business Insider several years ago. Back then, when Twitter was still called Twitter, it was possible for a profile of someone in a very niche industry to go viral, as Anna’s profile did. The subject of a profile rarely gets to confront its writer and ask, “What were you thinking?” or “Why did you do that?” But in this episode Anna and I finally have an opportunity to compare memories of our conversations, confess what each of us thought the other was after, and debate whether a profile of a woman can ever avoid reproducing the misogyny it aims to critique. 

Merve Emre: The last event that of our speaker series is always a special one; it involves someone who I have a very particular relationship with and often means doing something a bit uncomfortable. Anna is here because she wrote a profile of me for Business Insider, which ran with the headline—

Anna Silman: I didn’t pick the headline. I wanted to go with something more nuanced, but I think it was “How Merve Emre became the hottest—and most reviled—name in literary criticism.”

Together we lived through the virality of that profile. Since it came out, we’ve been talking about what it means to profile someone and what it means to try to present a coherent and controversial image of a person to the world. I have questions that I’ve been dying to ask you about that profile, so I thought that you would be the perfect guest to end our series. Do you feel nervous?

A little bit now, with that preamble.

We’ll start with a softball question. How did you get from college student at McGill University to where you are today, in my hot seat?

I studied English at McGill. Then, I received my Master’s in journalism at NYU in a program called Magazine and Digital Storytelling. I interned at The New York Observer and at New York magazine and started getting bylines. From there, I was at The Cut for six years, and then I went to Business Insider. I was there for four years doing long-form and investigative pieces, and now I am freelance.

I first read your profiles in The Cut when you asked me if I wanted to be your subject. I remember thinking that you always chose subjects that were a little bit spiky. Was this a correct read of what you were trying to do? How were you thinking of the first profiles you wrote?

Yeah, I think that is accurate. I did some garden-variety celebrity profiles, but I also profiled Anna Wiener, who wrote a book about Silicon Valley. I profiled Lauren Oyler, a critic who has written some viral pieces. Because The Cut was a general interest publication, the pieces had to have a larger takeaway that would be interesting to people who hadn’t read the books or didn’t know these writers. I look for subjects that can get into bigger questions and themes. It makes things more interesting if there’s a little bit of friction.

Friction between you and the person, or friction between that person and the world that they inhabit?

Friction between that person and the world. There was more friction in our interview than is typical for me in a profile. A bit of friction in an interview is always good. In fact, if there isn’t, sometimes I will try to create it, because that’s when the most interesting stuff comes up.

Did you feel there was friction between us?

Not in a bad way, but you were pushing back. We got into a meta conversation about the nature of profiling itself. We only went there because you asked me questions.

I want to touch on what you said about finding people who represent larger themes. How do you find those people, or do you first look for an interesting person and then elicit from that person a larger theme?

It depends. Sometimes a person is just clearly interesting; other times, they occupy an interesting space in the culture that is emblematic of a time or social shifts. I profiled a woman named Marissa Ross, who was a wine critic and part of the early wave of food social media. She dealt with a lot of online harassment. She has a big personality, and has been through many phases of her career. She was also an emblematic figure of early Instagram, when people were really self-promotional, and only later realized what a psychological toll it took. I felt like not only was she interesting, but by profiling her, I could touch on bigger questions about what it means to be a woman online.

Advertisement

Okay, so now tell me why my profile was a hard sell to your editor at Business Insider.

It felt like I was pitching a Cut story, but I had to convince the team that it was going to talk about business. In a way, it did: developing this writing program at Wesleyan, building a brand.

Did you come in with the “hot and reviled” angle?

I didn’t know you were reviled. I just knew that people at literary functions kept talking about you. There seemed to be a buzz around you, but you hadn’t been written about. That is always when my spidey senses prick up.

Before we decided to do this, we went for a Coca-Cola in the bar at Grand Central Terminal, and we talked on the phone another time.

Do you remember what I said to you to convince you?

Yes, I do remember. I think it shaped the personae that we adopt in the profile. You stressed to me that you had gone to McGill, where I had taught, and that your friends had been my students. The angle that really worked on me was you saying, I’m coming to you as a student, can you speak to me? I’m a complete sucker for that approach. I’m curious to know if that’s something you were doing deliberately.

If I’m trying to get someone to talk to me, I’ll lead with something we have in common. Once, I was reporting for a difficult story, and I found out that the woman I was talking to lived in the same small town as my aunt. We bonded over that. If I can find something that will make me feel more relatable to the person, I bring it up. When you’re trying to convince someone to do a profile, you’re asking them to give you a lot of trust and be vulnerable with you, and they don’t know what they’re going to come out of that experience with, so it’s a hard sell.

It’s funny because I was just rereading the beginning of Janet Malcolm’s The Journalist and the Murderer, and I was thinking about her meditation on how any journalist knows that what they’re doing is an act of great betrayal. In trying to interview another journalist, you speak to each other as colleagues, but even the person who knows better still gets seduced by the idea of having someone who will listen to them. I could have always said no, but I didn’t. I’m wondering if you have thoughts on why I didn’t.

I was not expecting you to say yes. I’ve put in a lot of legwork with people where it hasn’t worked out. It’s part of the process. I did get the sense that for you to do this, you would have to trust me, which is why we got to know each other a bit beforehand.

Okay, let’s talk about the interview. Do you remember coming to my house?

Yes.

Do you remember the first thing that we did?

I think we went and got a sandwich.

Then I remember sitting on my white couch in the living room, and you started asking questions about my family history. You said, Did you ever get in trouble as a teenager? Does that ring any bells?

It’s interesting that the parts that stood out for you, or where you thought I was angling at something, weren’t anomalies for me. I would always ask someone who’s very successful in their career if they ever had a rebellious phase.

Okay, so what do you remember? I have such a clear sequence of events in my mind, but, of course, you and I have completely different sequences in our minds.

I remember it was really hot that day. I was sweating, and you were not, which was freaking me out. I immediately realized that this was going to be fun. There was some good rapport. And you made me analyze these poems, which was like a nightmare.

It was one poem! You were an English major.

I didn’t do poetry.

I think I was explaining this class I was teaching, and I showed you the first poem, which is always the extraordinary poet Nicole Sealey, ventriloquizing the drag queen Pepper LaBeija. I always give it to my students because I think it’s fun and sassy. But tell me what you remember.

You know the dream where you are in school, and you’re about to go onstage and do a play, but you don’t know your lines, or you have a math test but you haven’t studied? I think it evoked that, this professor putting me on the spot about something I knew nothing about.

Advertisement

I think one of my flaws is that I always assume that people are as comfortable with me as I am with them. It’s really surprising for me to hear that you actually felt nervous.

I was nervous because when you’re interviewing someone who you respect, and who knows the game, that is always challenging. I didn’t feel like I could go toe-to-toe with you about the stuff that you write about, and that was intimidating. What if you felt that I didn’t understand your work, or wasn’t reading you right?

I thought we were fully equal. I just find myself so unintimidating.

We’re in the same industry, but you’re very successful in that industry. You were also a professor at a college that I went to. Obviously, I had the power in the sense that I was the one writing the piece, but there were other power dynamics there too.

How does that scene end up playing into the profile? When it came out, people really latched on to that scene.

While I really didn’t want to analyze a poem, I knew that it was good for the story. Any time there is a push-pull interplay between you and the person you’re interviewing, that’s good material. I’ve done interviews where you’re striving for any bit of color, any detail that will elevate it beyond that person’s talking points. So already, I knew that you were giving me material.

There is something interesting afoot when you’re writing about someone who knows the game you’re playing; they’re willing to play that game with you.

I find it way more intimidating to interview fellow writers or people whose work I admire. I’ve interviewed a lot of celebrities, and I never get as nervous as I do when it’s a peer.

I am not “media trained” in the way that we use that term today. I’m curious, what is your experience interviewing people who are exceptionally well trained to not give you anything?

Interviewing celebrities can be a slog, because they have prepared talking points. Their work may be interesting, but they themselves aren’t that interesting. I always prefer to interview someone who isn’t likely to have canned responses prepared.

So, back to the interview. My children came in, and one of my sons makes an appearance because he looks at you and says, “Literature is doomed.”

Yeah, that was also great color. When I’m writing a profile, I’m not just thinking about the thrust of the piece, but also what details will bring it to life. From the beginning, there were so many scenes that I knew would be vivid. It’s so rare that you get to meet a subject in their home, with their family, and that tells you so much about a person.

I should have been smarter and not let you in my home and not let you see my family.

I don’t know what you mean by smarter. It depends on what your goal would be. I don’t know what the reception was like for you, or if the stressful stuff was outweighed by positive attention that you got. I hope that it was the latter, but I don’t know if you regret doing the piece.

I don’t regret doing the piece. My barometer of everything is my friend Maggie Doherty, and she said, This does exactly what a profile should do. You have an interesting writer and an interesting subject, and you have tension. It’s not a hit piece, but it’s not a puff piece. There’s a productive ambivalence throughout. If that’s your standard for a profile, then I think it succeeds.

We had that conversation when we left my house, and I walked you to your hotel. We were walking across the New Haven Green near Yale, and that was when I turned to you with “a smile frozen on my face” and asked, “What are you doing here?”

Yeah, I expected you to just leave me at my hotel, but then you suggested we get a drink. I didn’t know how at the end of your rope you were. Often, when you think there’s a good interplay between you and the subject, you can leave it out. Way too many profiles have the “I” of the author when we don’t need it, but here it was clear that I was going to have to put myself in the story too.

Why was that so clear to you?

Because there was so much good dialogue. I didn’t know how I would capture a scene or you without including that.

I don’t remember feeling irritated. I really wanted to understand what you thought I would be representative of. That was the moment in our conversation when we started talking about misogyny, specifically the misogyny that women face in institutions like academia. I remember thinking clearly, I do not want to be representative of a neoliberal brand builder, nor do I want to be representative of a victim of institutional misogyny.

I think if I was earlier in my career and less experienced, there would have been a risk of the profile being like that. But I wanted to give the reader a sense of what an interesting person you were, which is divorced from what themes the piece might have explored. Of course, we had to talk about brand building, because Business Insider needed that. I knew we were going to talk about being a woman in academia, and misogyny, because it’s important and interesting to me, but I never come in knowing what a piece is going to say. I just had a sense of the bigger themes the piece might touch on. I didn’t think we would talk so much about the misogyny you’d faced at institutions, but I found that really fascinating, and it ended up becoming a big part of the piece.

It ends up becoming a big portion of it in part because of a different aspect of profiling, which is interviewing other people about me. How does asking other people about your subject change how you see your subject?

It can be really helpful. When you’re interviewing someone, you’re enmeshed in the story that they’re telling. When you hear from other people, you see if your intuitions about a person from this meeting are confirmed by other aspects of their lives. Talking to people confirmed some of the intuitions that I’d had while chatting with you, and that made me feel like it was okay to lean into them, because you can’t really know a person from hanging out with them for a day or two.

It’s funny because Doherty tells you, She’s really focused on her work, she doesn’t have many hobbies. I follow basketball, and she got hate mail from people that were like, “Fuck the Celtics” and from people defending me, saying, What are you talking about? She has a family, and what do you even know? It was wild to me that people were pulled into the orbit of the response in the way that they were.

I thought it would get like ten readers, because it’s a Business Insider piece about an academic, but the piece went viral. Our business model at the time had long features paywalled, so if you wanted to read the piece, you had to pay to subscribe to Business Insider. I remember we got hundreds of new signups. I could see from our behind-the-scenes metrics that it was doing very well, and it ignited a lot of chatter about things that hadn’t even occurred to me.

What hadn’t occurred to you?

I didn’t understand how academia worked, so I didn’t know it was going to prompt all these debates. It was a self-fulfilling thing, there are these examples of academics being crazy in the piece and the response to the piece was crazy.

I remember talking to Wesleyan’s president, Michael Roth, about this after it went viral and we had a good conversation about if the piece could get out of the misogyny that it’s setting itself up to critique. Did you feel like there were aspects of the piece, even inadvertently or subconsciously, that were feeding misogyny as opposed to pushing back against it?

I think any time you’re talking about a woman and her reception, you risk being part of the problem. It’s always hard to write about a woman’s appearance, especially because you’re a writer and academic. It’s unfair to you to talk about your appearance—and not the substance of your work. But at the same time, I felt like it didn’t make sense not to observe that there was a conversation about your appearance. It’s a fine line to walk, and I agonized about it.

Do you think it provoked the misogyny that it was critiquing?

Yeah, and unfortunately almost anything you write will provoke misogyny online right now. When I started to see the piece go viral, I got worried, because I didn’t want you, me, or any of the sources to get blowback. It’s always a risk when you put something into the public eye that it will be interpreted uncharitably and lead to all this ugly stuff.

Especially if it’s about a woman. I would say my real life, nondigital experience of the profile was very good. Basically, it was like, She’s an extremely hard worker who wants to build things. Who wouldn’t want that?

And now that you’re not in the thick of the drama, in hindsight, the piece just made you look iconic and cool.
